name: Mongolian khoomei overtone singing
lineage: Mongolian khoomei overtone-singing tradition. The technique produces a sustained chest-register fundamental while shaping the vocal tract to amplify upper partials of the harmonic series, generating a clearly audible whistle-tone melody floating above the fundamental. Khalkh-Mongol vocabulary distinguishes several techniques: kharkhiraa (low-register subharmonic kargyraa-equivalent), iisgerekh (mid-register sygyt-equivalent whistle-tone), shakhaa (constricted-throat variant), bagalzuuriin (deep throat-tension), and uyangiin (a singing-leaning lyrical variant). Performance contexts span solo concert, pastoral solo (a shepherd alone on the steppe), morin-khuur-accompanied ensemble, and the contemporary international touring circuit. Sundui, Tserendavaa, and Ganbold are the canonical twentieth-century khoomei masters; the post-1990 Mongolian state cultural-revival has produced a major export of khoomei performers internationally. The Smithsonian Folkways field recordings provide the principal Western-distributed documentation. Distinguished from Tuvan khoomei by Mongolian-Khalkh dialect-specific technique nomenclature and Mongolian-state-cultural-context performance framework (vs Tuvan-state-cultural-context); distinguished from Xhosa umngqokolo by Mongolian khoomei's throat-tension fundamental production (vs Xhosa's chest-register relaxed-fundamental); distinguished from Tibetan multiphonic yang chant by Mongolian khoomei's solo (vs ensemble-monastic) and secular (vs liturgical) configurations.
